subtopic_detail: Confirmatory testing before commencing targeted therapy for suspected pulmonary arterial hypertension
stem:
You are the registrar in a respiratory clinic. A 46-year-old woman is referred with 14 months of progressive exertional breathlessness, now limiting her to walking 200 m on the flat, and two episodes of light-headedness on climbing stairs.

She has limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis diagnosed 9 years ago with Raynaud phenomenon and sclerodactyly. She has never smoked and takes nifedipine and a proton pump inhibitor.

On examination there is a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, a left parasternal heave and a jugular venous pressure 5 cm above the sternal angle. The chest is clear. Spirometry is normal with a diffusing capacity 44 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography shows no interstitial disease and no evidence of emphysema. Ventilation perfusion scanning shows no mismatched segmental defects. Echocardiography estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressure at 62 mmHg with a dilated right ventricle and normal left ventricular size and function. Brain natriuretic peptide is 410 ng/L (<100).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, left parasternal heave, jugular venous pressure 5 cm above the sternal angle, chest clear, sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry normal with diffusing capacity 44 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography: no interstitial disease or emphysema. Ventilation perfusion scan: no mismatched segmental defects. Echocardiography: estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 62 mmHg, dilated right ventricle, normal left ventricular size and function. Brain natriuretic peptide 410 ng/L (<100)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Right heart catheterisation with vasoreactivity testing before any targeted therapy is commenced
options.rationale: Echocardiography estimates pulmonary pressures indirectly and cannot measure pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, which is what separates pre-capillary pulmonary arterial hypertension from post-capillary disease due to left heart pathology. Targeted vasodilator therapy is harmful in post-capillary disease and is only subsidised and justified once catheterisation has confirmed the haemodynamic diagnosis. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

options.text: Commence an endothelin receptor antagonist and arrange repeat echocardiography in 3 months
options.rationale: Starting targeted therapy on echocardiographic estimates alone risks treating post-capillary hypertension, in which pulmonary vasodilation increases transpulmonary flow into a congested left atrium and precipitates pulmonary oedema. It becomes appropriate once catheterisation confirms pre-capillary haemodynamics. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

options.text: Commence high dose calcium channel blocker therapy and arrange repeat echocardiography in 3 months
options.rationale: High dose calcium channel blockade benefits only the small minority who demonstrate acute vasoreactivity at catheterisation, and vasoreactive responders are very rare in connective tissue disease associated disease. Empirical use in non-responders causes systemic hypotension and right ventricular decompensation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

options.text: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant and arrange repeat imaging in 3 months
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is directed at chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, which the ventilation perfusion scan has effectively excluded by showing no mismatched segmental defects. It would be indicated if that scan had shown mismatched defects warranting pulmonary angiography. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

options.text: Commence long term oxygen therapy and arrange repeat arterial blood gas measurement in 3 months
options.rationale: Long term oxygen is prescribed for sustained resting hypoxaemia with an arterial oxygen tension at or below 55 mmHg, and her saturation is 94 per cent on room air. Oxygen would become appropriate if she developed resting hypoxaemia meeting those criteria. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary arterial hypertension complicating connective tissue disease, particularly systemic sclerosis, carries a worse prognosis than the idiopathic form, and an isolated reduction in diffusing capacity with normal lung volumes and no parenchymal disease is the classic early signal. The diagnostic pathway is deliberately sequential because the treatment is expensive, the drugs are hazardous in the wrong group, and the differential spans five distinct haemodynamic groups. Echocardiography is the screening test but systematically over and under-estimates pressures and cannot distinguish pre-capillary from post-capillary disease, which requires a measured pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. Before catheterisation, lung disease must be excluded by imaging and function testing and chronic thromboembolic disease by ventilation perfusion scanning, which is the test of choice because computed tomography angiography misses chronic organised thrombus. Screening annually with echocardiography and diffusing capacity in systemic sclerosis is recommended precisely because earlier treatment improves outcomes.
key_points: An isolated fall in diffusing capacity with normal volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease
Echocardiography screens but cannot separate pre-capillary from post-capillary hypertension
Right heart catheterisation with wedge pressure measurement is required before targeted therapy
Ventilation perfusion scanning excludes chronic thromboembolic disease more reliably than computed tomography angiography
Systemic sclerosis warrants annual screening because early treatment improves outcomes
explanation.pearls: Giving a pulmonary vasodilator to a patient whose hypertension is post-capillary can precipitate acute pulmonary oedema, which is why a measured wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg is required before targeted therapy begins.

subtopic_detail: Management of a congenital repolarisation disorder found during investigation of exertional syncope
stem:
You are the registrar in a cardiology clinic. A 19-year-old woman is referred after collapsing twice, once while swimming at a carnival and once when a fire alarm sounded unexpectedly at work.

On each occasion she lost consciousness without warning and recovered fully within a minute with no confusion afterward and no tongue biting or incontinence. Her mother describes brief jerking of the limbs during the second episode, lasting a few seconds while she was on the ground.

She takes no medicines and a urine drug screen is negative. A maternal aunt drowned at 22 while swimming in calm water. On examination the cardiovascular examination is normal with no murmur. Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium are within normal limits, as are thyroid function and full blood count. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart with normal biventricular function. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 496 ms and broad-based T waves in the precordial leads. An electroencephalogram is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 62/min, corrected QT interval 496 ms, broad-based precordial T waves. Echocardiography structurally normal with normal biventricular function. Potassium, magnesium, calcium, thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits. Electroencephalogram normal. Urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence an antiseizure medicine, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
options.rationale: The brief jerking described occurred after the patient was already on the ground and is typical of convulsive syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion rather than of a primary seizure. Rapid recovery without postictal confusion and a normal electroencephalogram argue against epilepsy, which is a common misdiagnosis in this condition. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Commence a non-selective beta blocker, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
options.rationale: Syncope triggered by swimming and by sudden auditory startle with a prolonged corrected QT interval and a family history of unexplained drowning indicates congenital long QT syndrome, in which beta blockade substantially reduces cardiac events. Non-selective agents such as nadolol and propranolol are preferred over selective agents, and cascade screening of first-degree relatives is essential because inheritance is autosomal dominant. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Arrange a permanent pacemaker, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
options.rationale: Pacing does not prevent the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that causes syncope in this condition and does not address the repolarisation abnormality. Pacing has a limited role in pause-dependent arrhythmia or in symptomatic bradycardia resulting from beta blockade. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Arrange catheter ablation, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for cardiac screening
options.rationale: Ablation targets a discrete arrhythmic focus or circuit, and this is a diffuse genetic disorder of ion channel repolarisation with no such target. Ablation would be appropriate for an accessory pathway or a focal ventricular tachycardia in a structurally normal heart. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Commence oral magnesium supplementation, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
options.rationale: Intravenous magnesium terminates established torsades de pointes but oral supplementation does not prevent events in congenital long QT syndrome, and her magnesium is already normal. Magnesium would be given acutely for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in progress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Congenital long QT syndrome is regularly misdiagnosed as epilepsy, because the cerebral hypoperfusion of a self-terminating polymorphic ventricular tachycardia produces brief limb jerking that observers describe as a fit. The distinguishing features are the abruptness of onset without aura, the speed of full recovery without postictal confusion, and above all the trigger. Trigger patterns map onto genotype with unusual fidelity: exertion and particularly swimming point to the potassium channel subtype, sudden auditory startle to the sodium-potassium subtype, and events during sleep or rest to the sodium channel subtype. A family history of drowning in a competent swimmer, of sudden infant death, or of unexplained single-vehicle accidents is highly relevant and should be sought explicitly. Beta blockade is the foundation of treatment, with non-selective agents outperforming selective ones, while an implantable defibrillator is reserved for aborted cardiac arrest or recurrent syncope despite adequate beta blockade, and avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs is a lifelong requirement.
key_points: Convulsive syncope with rapid full recovery and no postictal confusion suggests arrhythmia rather than epilepsy
Swimming and sudden auditory startle are characteristic triggers in specific genotypes
Family history of drowning, sudden infant death or unexplained accidents is highly relevant
Non-selective beta blockers are preferred over selective agents such as metoprolol
Cascade screening of first-degree relatives is required because inheritance is autosomal dominant
explanation.pearls: A competent swimmer who drowns in calm water should raise suspicion of the potassium channel subtype of long QT syndrome in the family, since swimming is its signature trigger and the diagnosis is frequently made only after a relative presents.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Long QT syndrome

subtopic_detail: Acute management when a febrile illness unmasks a type 1 coved ST elevation pattern
stem:
You are the registrar in an emergency department. A 32-year-old man of Vietnamese background presents with 2 days of fever and productive cough. He mentions that he briefly blacked out this morning while getting out of bed and hit his shoulder.

He has had two previous unexplained blackouts at night over 3 years, each attributed to a vasovagal cause. His older brother died suddenly in his sleep at 35 with a normal autopsy.

He takes no regular medicines. On examination the chest has coarse crackles at the right base and the cardiovascular examination is normal. Temperature is 39.1 °C. Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 104 beats per minute with coved ST elevation of 3 mm followed by an inverted T wave in leads V1 and V2, and a corrected QT interval of 400 ms. Potassium is 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), calcium and magnesium are within normal limits, and troponin is not elevated. An electrocardiogram from 2 years ago, taken when he was afebrile, showed only 1 mm of saddleback ST elevation in V1.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles at the right base, cardiovascular examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 104/min, coved ST elevation 3 mm with inverted T waves in V1 and V2, corrected QT interval 400 ms. Prior afebrile electrocardiogram 2 years ago: 1 mm saddleback ST elevation in V1 only. Chest radiograph right lower lobe consolidation. Potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), calcium and magnesium within normal limits, troponin not elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activate the catheter laboratory for primary percutaneous coronary intervention for anterior infarction
options.rationale: The ST elevation is confined to the right precordial leads with a coved morphology and inverted T waves, the troponin is not elevated and there is no chest pain, so this is not an occlusive infarction. Reperfusion would be correct for regional ST elevation with reciprocal change and a compatible ischaemic history. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Commence an intravenous amiodarone infusion and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral
options.rationale: Amiodarone does not prevent arrhythmia in this condition and sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmics accentuate the electrocardiographic pattern and the arrhythmic risk. Isoprenaline is the agent used for recurrent ventricular fibrillation in this setting, by increasing calcium current and heart rate. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Treat the fever aggressively with antipyretics and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral
options.rationale: Fever unmasks the type 1 coved pattern of Brugada syndrome by accentuating sodium channel dysfunction, and the arrhythmic risk is at its highest while the temperature is elevated, so aggressive antipyresis is itself an antiarrhythmic intervention. Continuous monitoring is required because ventricular fibrillation can occur without warning, and the syncope with a family history of nocturnal sudden death marks him as high risk. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Administer a flecainide challenge to confirm the diagnosis and admit to a monitored bed for observation
options.rationale: Provocation testing is used to unmask the pattern when the baseline tracing is non-diagnostic, and the diagnostic type 1 pattern is already present, so the challenge would add arrhythmic risk without diagnostic gain. It would be appropriate in an afebrile patient with only a saddleback pattern and a suggestive history. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Arrange urgent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral
options.rationale: Imaging is used to exclude structural mimics such as arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy but does not change the immediate priority of controlling the fever that is driving current risk. It would be a reasonable part of the subsequent workup once he is stable and afebrile. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

explanation.summary: Brugada syndrome is an inherited sodium channelopathy in which reduced inward sodium current creates a transmural voltage gradient in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing the coved ST elevation of the type 1 pattern and a substrate for phase 2 reentry and ventricular fibrillation. Its defining clinical feature is that the electrocardiogram is dynamic: the pattern waxes and wanes, and fever is the most important and most treatable unmasking factor because elevated temperature further impairs sodium channel kinetics. This makes a febrile illness a genuine emergency in an affected patient rather than an incidental finding, and antipyresis is therapeutic rather than merely symptomatic. Events characteristically occur at rest or during sleep and in males of South East Asian background at disproportionate rates, which is the opposite pattern to the exertional syncope of long QT syndrome or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Sodium channel blocking drugs, cocaine and excess alcohol all accentuate the phenotype and must be avoided lifelong, while an implantable defibrillator remains the only proven treatment for those with aborted arrest or arrhythmic syncope.
key_points: Fever unmasks the type 1 coved pattern and markedly increases arrhythmic risk
Aggressive antipyresis is an antiarrhythmic intervention, not merely symptomatic care
Events occur at rest or during sleep rather than with exertion
Sodium channel blockers, cocaine and excess alcohol accentuate the phenotype and are avoided
An implantable defibrillator is the only proven therapy after arrhythmic syncope or aborted arrest
explanation.pearls: Give paracetamol early and at full dose for any febrile illness in a patient with a Brugada pattern, and record a repeat electrocardiogram once afebrile, because the type 1 morphology may disappear entirely and the diagnosis be wrongly discarded.

subtopic_detail: Timing intervention for rheumatic mitral stenosis presenting with pulmonary oedema in mid-pregnancy
stem:
You are the registrar in a coronary care unit. A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy is admitted with 4 days of worsening breathlessness, now orthopnoeic and unable to lie flat.

She arrived in Australia from the Pacific at 14 and recalls being told as a child that she had a heart murmur after a febrile illness with sore joints. She has had no cardiology follow-up.

She has responded partially to intravenous frusemide and oxygen in the emergency department. On examination the pulse is 112 beats per minute and irregularly irregular. There is a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. There are crackles to the mid zones bilaterally. Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation at 112 beats per minute. Transthoracic echocardiography reports a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm2 with a mean gradient of 16 mmHg, pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no mitral regurgitation, no left atrial thrombus and estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 58 mmHg. Foetal cardiotocography is normal and growth is on the 45th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 112/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 93% on 4 L/min oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Loud first heart sound, opening snap, low-pitched mid-diastolic apical murmur, bilateral crackles to the mid zones
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: atrial fibrillation at 112/min. Echocardiography: mitral valve area 0.9 cm2, mean gradient 16 mmHg, pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no mitral regurgitation, no left atrial thrombus, estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 58 mmHg. Cardiotocography normal, growth 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Open mitral valve replacement on cardiopulmonary bypass after rate control and anticoagulation
options.rationale: Cardiopulmonary bypass in pregnancy carries foetal mortality of roughly 20 to 30 per cent through non-pulsatile placental perfusion, so it is reserved for valves unsuitable for percutaneous treatment. Replacement would be appropriate for a heavily calcified valve, significant mitral regurgitation or left atrial thrombus. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

options.text: Continued diuresis with beta blockade alone and planned reassessment in the third trimester
options.rationale: Medical therapy is the correct first step but she has already failed it while cardiac output demands continue to rise until around 32 weeks, so deferring intervention allows further deterioration. Ongoing medical management alone would be reasonable for moderate stenosis with symptoms controlled on rate control and diuretics. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

options.text: Emergency caesarean birth at 26 weeks followed by valve intervention in the postpartum period
options.rationale: Delivery at 26 weeks commits the infant to extreme prematurity and the immediate haemodynamic stress of birth and autotransfusion is poorly tolerated in severe mitral stenosis. Delivery would be the priority if the foetus were near term or if maternal collapse were imminent and irreversible. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

options.text: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty after rate control and anticoagulation are established
options.rationale: Severe mitral stenosis with pulmonary oedema refractory to medical therapy in pregnancy warrants mechanical relief of the obstruction, and pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no regurgitation and no left atrial thrombus make this valve ideally suited to balloon valvuloplasty. The percutaneous route avoids cardiopulmonary bypass, which carries substantial foetal loss rates, and rate control plus anticoagulation are established first because the new atrial fibrillation is driving the decompensation. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

options.text: Direct current cardioversion to sinus rhythm alone with anticoagulation and no valve intervention
options.rationale: Restoring sinus rhythm improves diastolic filling time and is a valuable adjunct, but it leaves a valve area of 0.9 cm2 obstructing flow and recurrence of atrial fibrillation is likely while the left atrium remains pressurised. Cardioversion alone would suffice if the underlying valve lesion were mild. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

explanation.summary: Rheumatic mitral stenosis remains an important cause of maternal morbidity in Australia, disproportionately affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and people who grew up in the Pacific and South East Asia, and pregnancy is frequently the event that unmasks it. The physiology explains why: cardiac output rises by up to half by the early third trimester and tachycardia shortens diastole, and since the stenotic valve fills only during diastole, both changes raise left atrial pressure steeply. New atrial fibrillation compounds this by removing atrial systole and shortening filling time further, which is often the final trigger for pulmonary oedema. Medical management with rate control, cautious diuresis and anticoagulation is first-line, but failure of medical therapy in severe stenosis before term requires mechanical relief because the haemodynamic burden will only increase. Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty is strongly preferred over surgery, with abdominal shielding and minimised screening time, and valve morphology determines suitability, while anticoagulation matters because left atrial stasis with atrial fibrillation carries a high thromboembolic risk in an already prothrombotic pregnancy.
key_points: Cardiac output rises through pregnancy and tachycardia shortens diastolic filling, worsening the gradient
New atrial fibrillation removes atrial systole and often precipitates decompensation
Balloon valvuloplasty suits pliable non-calcified valves without regurgitation or left atrial thrombus
Cardiopulmonary bypass carries foetal mortality of roughly 20 to 30 per cent and is a second choice
Anticoagulate for atrial fibrillation with mitral stenosis regardless of any risk score
explanation.pearls: Atrial fibrillation with rheumatic mitral stenosis is an absolute indication for warfarin rather than a direct oral anticoagulant, since the direct agents have not been shown safe in this valve lesion and are specifically excluded from that indication.

subtopic_detail: Deciding between infective and immune causes of diarrhoea on checkpoint inhibitor therapy
stem:
You are the registrar in an oncology day unit. A 61-year-old man receiving combination immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy for metastatic melanoma presents 5 weeks after his second cycle with 8 days of increasing diarrhoea, now 9 loose stools daily with abdominal cramping and visible blood on two occasions.

He has been opening his bowels twice overnight. He has had no recent travel, no antibiotic exposure and no unwell contacts, and no fever at home.

On examination the abdomen is soft with generalised tenderness and no guarding and no rebound. Bowel sounds are present. Stool testing is negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin, negative on bacterial culture and negative on viral and parasite polymerase chain reaction panel. Cytomegalovirus serology shows past exposure. C-reactive protein is 78 mg/L (<5), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 122 g/L (130-180) and faecal calprotectin markedly elevated. Computed tomography of the abdomen shows diffuse colonic wall thickening with mesenteric fat stranding and no perforation and no abscess.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness, no guarding, no rebound, bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: Stool Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, bacterial culture negative, viral and parasite panel negative. C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (<5), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 122 g/L (130-180), faecal calprotectin markedly elevated. Computed tomography: diffuse colonic wall thickening with mesenteric fat stranding, no perforation or abscess
data_table.Treatment: Combination immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, second cycle 5 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue immunotherapy and commence loperamide with dietary modification and outpatient review
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are appropriate for mild grade 1 diarrhoea but risk masking progression and precipitating toxic dilatation in established immune colitis. Loperamide would be reasonable for fewer than four extra stools daily with no blood, no nocturnal symptoms and normal inflammatory markers. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

options.text: Withhold immunotherapy and commence oral vancomycin with repeat stool toxin testing in 48 hours
options.rationale: Clostridioides difficile is an important differential in this population but the toxin assay is negative and there has been no antibiotic exposure or healthcare contact to support it. Vancomycin would be indicated if toxin or nucleic acid testing were positive alongside compatible symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Withhold immunotherapy and commence infliximab as initial therapy with gastroenterology referral
options.rationale: Infliximab is the standard second-line agent for immune colitis but is reserved for patients who fail to improve after roughly 3 days of adequate corticosteroid. Starting it first exposes the patient to infection risk before establishing whether steroid alone will control the colitis. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

options.text: Withhold immunotherapy and arrange urgent colonoscopy with biopsies before commencing any treatment
options.rationale: Endoscopy usefully assesses severity and excludes cytomegalovirus colitis, but deferring treatment until it can be arranged risks progression in a patient with an established clinical and radiological diagnosis. Colonoscopy should proceed alongside, not before, corticosteroid therapy in grade 3 disease. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

options.text: Withhold immunotherapy and commence high dose systemic corticosteroid with gastroenterology referral
options.rationale: Nine stools daily with blood, nocturnal symptoms and radiological colitis after infection has been excluded is grade 3 immune-related colitis, which requires immunotherapy to be withheld and high dose corticosteroid started promptly. Delay is the principal driver of perforation and death in this complication, so treatment begins on clinical and radiological grounds rather than awaiting endoscopy. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

explanation.summary: Immune-related colitis is among the most common serious toxicities of checkpoint inhibition and is substantially more frequent and more severe with combination cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 and programmed death 1 blockade than with either agent alone. Onset is typically weeks to months after starting treatment and can occur after the drug has been stopped, since the immune activation outlasts drug exposure, so the diagnosis must be considered in any patient who has ever received these agents. Grading drives management: mild disease is managed symptomatically while continuing treatment, moderate disease prompts withholding the drug and starting corticosteroid, and severe disease requires admission, high dose corticosteroid and early escalation. Infection must be excluded because the treatment is immunosuppression, but exclusion should not delay therapy when the clinical picture is convincing, and cytomegalovirus reactivation should be reconsidered in anyone who fails to respond. Corticosteroid non-response by around day 3 is the trigger for infliximab or vedolizumab, and untreated or slowly treated colitis progresses to perforation, which carries high mortality in this population.
key_points: Combination checkpoint blockade causes more frequent and more severe colitis than single agent therapy
Onset is typically weeks to months after initiation and can follow drug cessation
Blood in stool, nocturnal symptoms and more than six extra stools daily indicate severe disease
Exclude infection but do not delay corticosteroid when the clinical picture is convincing
Escalate to infliximab or vedolizumab if there is no response after about 3 days of corticosteroid
explanation.pearls: Reconsider cytomegalovirus colitis by requesting tissue polymerase chain reaction on colonic biopsies in any patient whose immune colitis fails to respond to corticosteroid, because serology showing past exposure does not distinguish latent infection from active reactivation unmasked by immunosuppression.
